passages.t: Locusts announced, and a story for the children
passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, that I may perform these miraculous signs of Mine among them, and that you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians when I performed miraculous signs among them, so that all of you may know that I am the LORD” (verses 1-2).

Moses and Aaron say to Pharaoh, “How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me? Let My people go, so that they may worship Me” (verse 3). If he refuses, locusts will come tomorrow. “They will cover the face of the land so that no one can see it. They will devour whatever is left after the hail” (verse 5). Then Moses turns and leaves (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
There is a new purpose here. Earlier plagues were so that Pharaoh and Egypt would know the LORD. Now they are also so that Israel will tell their children and grandchildren. The plagues become a story for Israel's future, to be told at the table for generations.

‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself?’ The issue was never only the slaves. It was pride, a king who would not bow to anyone.

Locust swarms were one of the great terrors of the ancient world, and they still strike parts of Africa and Asia. In its swarming stage the desert locust gathers in huge numbers, rides the wind for long distances, and strips crops and trees of everything green. After the hail, the locusts will eat whatever is left.

And Moses does not wait for an answer. He turns and walks out.
passages.later:
Israel's law tells parents to answer their children with this story: “In the future, when your son asks, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?’ then you are to tell him, ‘We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand’” (Deuteronomy 6:20-21).

The psalmist promises the same: “We will not hide them from their children, but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might, and the wonders He has performed” (Psalm 78:4).
passages.asks: God wanted this story told to children and grandchildren. Ask what story of God's faithfulness you are passing on to the next generation. And ask whether your children, or the young people near you, have ever heard it from you.

passages.t: The officials plead, and Pharaoh bargains
passages.happening:
“Pharaoh’s officials asked him, ‘How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God. Do you not yet realize that Egypt is in ruins?’” (verse 7).

Pharaoh calls Moses back. “Go, worship the LORD your God,” he says. “But who exactly will be going?” (verse 8). “We will go with our young and old,” Moses replies. “We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD” (verse 9).

Pharaoh mocks, “May the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones. Clearly you are bent on evil. No, only the men may go” (verses 10-11). And Moses and Aaron are driven out.
passages.hearers:
Now Pharaoh's own court turns against him. His officials see what he will not: ‘Egypt is in ruins’. They beg him to let the people go.

Pharaoh tries a new bargain. Let the men go, and keep the women and children. Men who leave their families behind will have to come back. It is a leash.

Pharaoh's words in verse 10 twist a blessing into a sneer. ‘May the LORD be with you’ was a blessing. On his lips it means: never.

Moses' answer matters. Everyone goes, young and old, sons and daughters. Worship in Israel is never for the men alone, or for the grown-ups alone. It belongs to the whole people.
passages.later:
When Israel later gathers to hear God's law, the whole people are there: “men, women, children, and the foreigners within your gates” (Deuteronomy 31:12).

Peter says on the day of Pentecost, “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off” (Acts 2:39).
passages.asks: Moses would not leave the children behind. Ask whether the young ones in your church and your home are truly included in its worship. And ask what it would mean for you to bring the whole of your life to God, and not only the part you choose.

passages.t: Locusts, until nothing green is left
passages.happening:
“So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts” (verse 13).

“They covered the face of all the land until it was black, and they consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt” (verse 15).

Pharaoh says, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you. Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me” (verses 16-17). Moses prays. God turns the wind, “a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea” (verse 19).

“But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let the Israelites go” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The text names the means: an east wind, blowing all day and all night, brings the locusts from the desert. Then God sends a strong wind from the west. In Hebrew it is a ‘sea wind’, because the Mediterranean lay to the west. It sweeps them into the Red Sea. The Bible does not set God's action against the wind. God uses the wind.

Pharaoh calls the locusts ‘this death’. For a land that lived on its crops, that is what they were.

A word runs through this chapter: ‘left’. The locusts eat what the hail ‘left’. Not one locust is ‘left’ when the wind takes them away. And later Moses will say not a hoof will be ‘left’ behind. Egypt is being emptied, while Israel is kept whole.

Once again Pharaoh says ‘I have sinned’. Once again the relief comes. And once again his heart is hardened.
passages.later:
The prophet Joel later used a locust plague as his picture of the day of the LORD, “a day of darkness and gloom”, with an army “such as never was of old” (Joel 2:2), in words that echo this chapter.

The psalm remembers: “He gave their crops to the grasshopper, the fruit of their labor to the locust” (Psalm 78:46).
passages.hard:
Why should the ordinary people of Egypt suffer for Pharaoh's stubbornness? The plagues fall on the whole land: fields, animals, homes and bodies. It is fair to ask why farmers and servants should lose everything because their king would not listen.

Several answers are given. The ancient world assumed a bond between a ruler and his people that modern people do not, and Pharaoh's officials clearly understand in verse 7 that his choices are ruining them all. Exodus also presents the oppression as the nation's, not only the king's. Pharaoh “commanded all his people” to throw the Hebrew boys into the Nile (1:22), and the Egyptians “worked the Israelites ruthlessly” (1:13). The plagues came step by step, with warnings, and when a warning offered a way to escape, some Egyptians took it (9:20). Many Egyptians later show favor to Israel (11:3; 12:36).

None of this makes the suffering small, and the text does not pretend it is. What it insists on is that the one who kept it going was Pharaoh, whose own court begged him to give way.

And the rest of Scripture refuses to write Egypt off. Isaiah looks ahead to a day when “the LORD will strike Egypt with a plague; He will strike them but heal them. They will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them” (Isaiah 19:22). The God who judged Egypt did not stop intending good for it.
passages.asks: The officials saw that Egypt was in ruins, and the king would not listen. Ask whether there are people around you suffering because of a choice you refuse to change. And ask what it would take for you to listen to those who see more clearly than you.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that darkness may spread over the land of Egypt” (verse 21). It will be ‘a palpable darkness’.

“So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days. No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings” (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
This is the ninth plague, the last of the third group, and like the third in each group it comes with no warning.

A ‘palpable darkness’ means a darkness you could feel. For three days, no one could see anyone else, and no one moved.

The darkness struck at the heart of Egypt's religion. The sun god Re, often joined with Amun as Amun-Re, was among the greatest of Egypt's gods, and one of Pharaoh's official titles was Son of Re. For three days the god whose rising and setting ordered the Egyptian world did not appear, while the slaves had light. The text never names Re. A first hearer could hardly miss the point.

Many readers connect this darkness with the khamsin, a hot spring wind off the desert that can fill the air with dust thick enough to hide the sun for days. If so, the timing fits the spring and the coming Passover. But the text's interest is in what no wind explains: it comes when Moses lifts his hand, it lasts three days, and Israel has light where they live.
passages.later:
The psalm sums it up: “He sent darkness, and it became dark” (Psalm 105:28).

When Jesus was crucified, “From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land” (Mark 15:33). In Egypt darkness came before the death of the firstborn. At the cross it came while God's own Son was dying. The Gospels do not cite Exodus here, so it is an echo readers have noticed, not a stated fulfillment.

Jesus says, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness” (John 8:12). Paul writes that God “has rescued us from the dominion of darkness” (Colossians 1:13).
passages.asks: Egypt sat in darkness while Israel had light. Ask where darkness is pressing on you, or on someone you love. And ask what it would mean to trust the God who gives light in his people's homes, even when all around is dark.

passages.t: ‘Not a hoof will be left behind’
passages.happening:
Pharaoh calls Moses: “Go, worship the LORD. Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind” (verse 24).

Moses answers, “Even our livestock must go with us; not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God, and we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive” (verse 26).

“But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let them go” (verse 27). “Depart from me!” Pharaoh says. “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die” (verse 28). “‘As you say,’ Moses replied, ‘I will never see your face again’” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Pharaoh's last offer: everyone may go, but leave the animals. Families who leave their herds behind will have to come back. It is one more leash.

Moses refuses any leash. ‘Not a hoof will be left behind.’ His reason is worship. Israel does not yet know what God will ask of them in sacrifice until they arrive. So everything must come.

Watch the bargaining from the beginning. Sacrifice here in Egypt (8:25). Go, but not far (8:28). Only the men (10:11). Everyone but the animals (10:24). Pharaoh keeps trying to keep something back. Moses will not let anything stay in his hand.

Then the break. In a royal court, to see the king's face meant to be welcome. Pharaoh's words are a formal banishment with a death threat. Moses agrees.

There is a bitter irony here. Pharaoh threatens death if they meet again. But the next death to come will fall on Pharaoh's own house.
passages.later:
Paul urges believers to give God everything, not part: “offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (Romans 12:1).

Hebrews says of Moses that “By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger” (Hebrews 11:27).
passages.asks: Pharaoh offered everything but the animals; Moses said, ‘Not a hoof will be left behind.’ Ask what you are trying to keep back from God, one small part of your life held in reserve. And ask what it would mean to bring all of it, not knowing yet what God will ask.
